what_its_for: Opicapone is used along with levodopa/carbidopa (your main Parkinson's medicine) to help control Parkinson's disease symptoms. It helps reduce 'off' periods — those times during the day when your Parkinson's symptoms come back or get worse because your levodopa medicine is wearing off. Opicapone works by blocking an enzyme that breaks down levodopa, helping your levodopa last longer and work better.
how_to_take: Take opicapone by mouth once a day at bedtime, at least one hour BEFORE or one hour AFTER your last levodopa/carbidopa dose of the day. Swallow the capsule whole — do not crush, chew, or open it. Take it at the same time every night to help you remember. You can take it with or without food, but taking it near bedtime (away from your levodopa dose) is very important for it to work properly.
dosing: The usual dose is ONE 50 mg capsule taken by mouth once every night at bedtime. Your doctor may adjust your levodopa dose after you start this medicine. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Do not take more or less than prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip it and take your next dose at your regular bedtime the following night. Do NOT take two doses to make up for the missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store opicapone at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Keep it in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicines down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about a medicine take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking opicapone at the same time as your levodopa/carbidopa dose — always separate them by at least one hour. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you, as it can cause sudden sleepiness or dizziness. Avoid standing up too quickly, as this medicine can lower your blood pressure and make you feel faint. Avoid drinking alcohol, as it may worsen dizziness or drowsiness. Tell your doctor or pharmacist before taking any new medicines, including supplements, as some drugs (like certain antidepressants called MAO inhibitors) can cause dangerous interactions.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience: sudden urges to fall asleep during daily activities, uncontrolled movements (twisting or writhing), fainting or severe dizziness when standing, confusion or hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there), unusual strong urges (such as gambling, shopping, eating, or sexual urges), skin rash or signs of allergic reaction, very high fever with stiff muscles (a rare but serious reaction called neuroleptic malignant syndrome), or dark brown or black urine (this is usually harmless but worth reporting). Also call your doctor if your Parkinson's symptoms are not improving or getting worse.
when_it_works: You may start to notice improvement in your 'on' time (when your Parkinson's medicine is working well) within the first few weeks of treatment. However, it may take several weeks to feel the full benefit. Keep taking it every day as prescribed, even if you do not notice changes right away. Do not stop taking it suddenly without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Older adults: Use with caution, as side effects like dizziness, fainting, and confusion may be more common. Kidney problems: No dose adjustment is usually needed for mild to moderate kidney problems. Liver problems: Opicapone should NOT be used if you have moderate to severe liver disease — tell your doctor if you have any liver conditions. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: It is not known if opicapone is safe during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Talk to your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding before taking this medicine. Children: This medicine is not approved for use in children.
